title: Keeping Comparable Company Sets Current
answer: Keeping comparable company sets current is the work of maintaining the peer groups that valuation, benchmarking and screening depend on. In an AI-focused finance workflow the set drifts constantly, because companies enter the space through acquisitions, spin-outs and reclassification, and because a peer that was a pure software name two years ago may now earn most of its revenue from model serving. The task covers listed instruments, private rounds that change the listed comparables, and the filings that record the change. It sits between research and data operations, and it is usually owned by whoever publishes the multiples.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Keeping comparable company sets current is the work of maintaining the peer groups that valuation, benchmarking and screening depend on. In an AI-focused finance workflow the set drifts constantly, because companies enter the space through acquisitions, spin-outs and reclassification, and because a peer that was a pure software name two years ago may now earn most of its revenue from model serving. The task covers listed instruments, private rounds that change the listed comparables, and the filings that record the change. It sits between research and data operations, and it is usually owned by whoever publishes the multiples.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a company master with stable identifiers, a mapping from each company to one or more peer sets, and a dated history of every membership change. Prices and fundamentals arrive from market data feeds, while corporate actions and ownership changes arrive from filings and exchange notices. This site tracks 117 listed AI-related instruments with daily prices and 514 company pages, which is the scale at which manual review stops being reliable. A scheduler runs the refresh, a queue holds the exceptions, and a review interface lets an analyst accept or reject each proposed change.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: An agent workflow typically watches for triggers, such as a merger filing, a ticker change, a segment reclassification or a sharp shift in revenue mix, and proposes a membership edit with the evidence attached. Rules handle the mechanical cases, and a model handles the ambiguous ones by reading filing text and comparing business descriptions. Every proposal carries a confidence and a reason, and a human signs off before the peer set is republished. The output is a versioned set with an audit trail, so any multiple can be traced back to the membership that produced it.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are stale membership, silent edits and peer sets that quietly flatter a valuation. Controls include dated versions, a named approver for each change, and a rule that no company enters or leaves a set without a cited source. Provenance matters because a benchmark number is only as good as the group behind it, and this site already tracks 401 merger and acquisition filings and 150 active AI lawsuits, both of which can move a company out of a peer group. Licensing and redistribution terms for the underlying data also constrain what can be shown. Nothing here is investment advice, and the peer set is a research input rather than a recommendation.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect more of the refresh to be automated, with agents drafting the change, citing the filing and routing it for approval, and with humans handling only contested cases. Peer sets will likely become more granular and more temporary, assembled for a question rather than maintained as a fixed list. The harder problem is not detection but definition, since what counts as an AI comparable keeps moving. Teams that keep a clean, dated history of membership changes will be able to answer that question later, and teams that overwrite their sets will not.
